title: The dove, the raven and the charge of forgery
source_text: Ἔῤῥιψε δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος τὰ περὶ τῆς περιστερᾶς, ἵνα δόξῃ ἀνεγνωκέναι τὸ βιβλίον τὴν Γένεσιν, οὐδὲν δυνηθεὶς εἰπεῖν πρὸς τὸ ἐλέγξαι πλασματῶδες τὸ κατὰ τὴν περιστεράν. εἶθ᾿ ὡς ἔθος αὐτῷ ἐστιν ἐπὶ τὸ γελοιότερον μεταφράζειν τὰ γεγραμμένα, „τὸν κόρακα“ εἰς κορώνην μετείληφε καὶ οἴεται ταῦτα Μωϋσέα ἀναγεγραφέναι, ῥᾳδιουργοῦντα τὰ κατὰ τὸν παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι Δευκαλίωνα· εἰ μὴ ἄρα οὐδὲ Μωϋσέως οἴεται εἶναι τὴν γραφὴν ἀλλά τινων πλειόνων· τοιοῦτον γὰρ δηλοῖ τὸ παραχαράττοντες καὶ ῥᾳδιουργοῦντες τὸν Δευκαλίωνα, καὶ τοῦτο· οὐ γὰρ οἶμαι προσεδόκησαν ὅτι ταῦτ᾿ εἰς φῶς πρόεισι. πῶς δ᾿ οἱ ὅλῳ ἔθνει διδόντες γράμματα οὐ προσεδόκησαν αὐτὰ εἰς φῶς προελθεῖν, οἳ καὶ ἐπροφήτευσαν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι τὴν θεοσέβειαν ταύτην κηρυχθήσεσθαι; ὁ δ᾿ Ἰησοῦς τὸ „ἀρθήσεται ἀφ᾿ ὑμῶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ δοθήσεται ἔθνει ποιοῦντι τοὺς καρποὺς αὐτῆς“ Ἰουδαίοις λέγων τί ἄλλο ᾠκονόμει ἢ εἰς φῶς αὐτὸς θείᾳ δυνάμει προαγαγεῖν πᾶσαν τὴν Ἰουδαϊκὴν γραφὴν, περιέχουσαν μυστήρια τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ βασιλείας; εἶτα ἐὰν μὲν τὰς Ἑλλήνων θεογονίας καὶ τὰς περὶ θεῶν δώδεκα ἱστορίας ἀναγινώσκωσι, σεμνοποιοῦσιν αὐτὰς ταῖς ἀλληγορίαις, ἐὰν δὲ τὰ ἡμέτερα διασύρειν βούλωνται, ἀτεχνῶς φασι παισὶ νηπίοις αὐτὰ μεμυθολογῆσθαι.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus threw in (ἔρριψε, ῥίπτω) the things about the dove (περιστερά), in order to seem (δόξῃ) to have read (ἀνεγνωκέναι) the book Genesis, having been able to say nothing towards refuting (ἐλέγξαι) as fictitious (πλασματῶδες) the matter of the dove. Then, as is his custom (ἔθος) to paraphrase (μεταφράζειν) the written things toward the more laughable (γελοιότερον), he changed (μετείληφε) 'the raven' (κόραξ) into a crow (κορώνη), and he supposes Moses wrote these things, tampering with (ῥᾳδιουργοῦντα) the things about the Deucalion among the Greeks; unless perhaps he thinks the writing is not even of Moses but of some several (persons) (τινων πλειόνων); for such is shown by 'counterfeiting (παραχαράττοντες, plural) and tampering with Deucalion', and this: 'for I do not think they expected (προσεδόκησαν) that these things would come out into light (εἰς φῶς πρόεισι)'. And how did those who gave letters/writings (γράμματα) to a whole nation (ἔθνει) not expect them to come out to light, who also prophesied (ἐπροφήτευσαν) that this piety/worship of God (θεοσέβεια) would be proclaimed (κηρυχθήσεσθαι) to all the nations? And Jesus, saying to Jews the 'the kingdom of God will be taken (ἀρθήσεται) from you and will be given to a nation making its fruits', what else was he arranging (ᾠκονόμει, οἰκονομέω) than himself by divine power (θείᾳ δυνάμει) to bring forward into light the whole Jewish scripture (γραφή), containing mysteries (μυστήρια) of the kingdom of God? Then, if they read the theogonies (θεογονίας) of Greeks and the histories about twelve gods, they make them solemn/dignified (σεμνοποιοῦσιν) by allegories (ἀλληγορίαις); but if they wish to disparage (διασύρειν) ours, they say these were simply (ἀτεχνῶς) mythologised (μεμυθολογῆσθαι) to infant children (παισὶ νηπίοις).
pass_b_english: Celsus has tossed in the matter of the dove so as to seem to have read the book of Genesis, though he could say nothing to prove that the story of the dove is a fiction (Genesis 8:8–12). Then, since it is his habit to reword what is written so as to make it more laughable, he has changed “the raven” into a crow (Genesis 8:7), and he thinks that Moses recorded these things while tampering with the story of Deucalion told among the Greeks, unless perhaps he does not even think the writing is by Moses, but by a number of people. For that is what these words show: “counterfeiting and tampering with the story of Deucalion,” and these as well: “For I do not suppose they expected that these things would come to light.”

But how could those who gave writings to a whole nation not expect them to come to light, when they even prophesied that this worship of God would be preached to all the nations? And when Jesus said to the Jews, “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21:43), what else was he arranging but that he himself, by divine power, should bring into the light the whole of the Jewish Scripture, which contains mysteries of the kingdom of God? Then, if they read the theogonies of the Greeks and the stories about the twelve gods, they lend them dignity by allegories; but when they wish to mock ours, they say these were simply told as myths to little children.

Joined the 'unless perhaps' fragment to its main sentence
τοιοῦτον γὰρ δηλοῖ τὸ …: subject is the quoted words, not Celsus; rendered 'that is what these words show' and dropped the supplied 'they were'
Aligned the two repeated Celsus quotations with the 4.41 wording ('the story of Deucalion', 'I do not suppose')
Translator note: recorded the echo of Celsus's ἀτεχνῶς παισὶ νηπίοις ἐμυθολόγησαν (4.41)

Copy-text: staged source_4.json section 42 (Koetschau 4.42). Celsus’s phrases repeated from 4.41: παραχαράττοντες καὶ ῥᾳδιουργοῦντες τὸν Δευκαλίωνα (‘counterfeiting’ is the coin-debasing word) and οὐ γὰρ οἶμαι προσεδόκησαν ὅτι ταῦτ᾿ εἰς φῶς πρόεισιν; worded here exactly as in the 4.41 rendering (‘the story of Deucalion’, ‘I do not suppose’) so the reader sees the same quotation. Origen’s argument turns on the plural participles and the plural ‘they expected’ (several authors, not Moses alone). ‘The raven’ is marked as Scripture by the edition (Genesis 8:7 LXX τὸν κόρακα); Celsus wrote κορώνη, ‘crow’. Matthew 21:43 quoted exactly as in the Gospel text. Uncited allusion: the prophecy that ‘this worship of God would be preached to all the nations’ is a general reference to the prophets (compare Genesis 22:18; Isaiah 2:2–3), not a quotation, so no inline citation. The subject ‘they’ in the last sentence shifts from Celsus to pagan critics generally, as in the Greek; ‘simply told as myths to little children’ turns Celsus’s own words from 4.41 (ἀτεχνῶς παισὶ νηπίοις ἐμυθολόγησαν) back on them.
